text.text: Excess mortality can be estimated from crude death counts or from age-standardised mortality rates (ASMRs).

Although both approaches are widely used, their analytical relationship and the effects of methodological choices such as standard population, age-group definition, and baseline selection are not always explicitly considered.

The analytical relationship between relative excess mortality based on death counts and ASMRs was derived and both approaches were applied to mortality in Germany during the COVID19 pandemic 2020-2023.
Expected mortality was estimated by linear extrapolation of pre-pandemic trends.
ASMR calculations were repeated using different standard populations, age-group definitions, open-ended age groups, and reference periods.
Death-count-and ASMR-based P-scores were analytically equivalent when the age distribution of the standard population corresponded to that of the population under study.
Empirically, both approaches yielded closely corresponding estimates for Germany.
The effect of the standard population depended on the age distribution of excess mortality and was particularly pronounced in 2020, when excess mortality was concentrated at older ages.
The definition of the open-ended age group had an additional effect: aggregating ages 80+ altered the pre-pandemic ASMR trend, and consequently changed the estimated excess mortality.
Variation of the pre-pandemic reference period substantially affected P-scores, but death-count-and ASMR-based estimates changed in a closely corresponding manner.
Relative excess mortality derived from death counts and ASMRs is closely related, and differences between the approaches can be explained by their underlying weighting and baseline assumptions.
For trend-based excess mortality estimation, the standard population, age-group definition, and baseline specification are therefore integral methodological choices.

Death counts provide a simple and transparent reference measure for analyses within a single population, whereas age-standardised estimates require careful consideration of these additional assumptions.
Excess mortality is defined as the degree to which the observed number of deaths exceeds the number expected under a counterfactual baseline.

It has been widely used to assess the overall mortality impact of the COVID-19 pandemic because it is based on all-cause mortality and is therefore independent of the classification and reporting of individual causes of death.
Different mortality measures can be used for the calculation of excess mortality.
The most direct approach is based on crude death counts, i.e. the absolute number of deaths in a population during a specified period.
Studies comparing multiple countries use death counts, as these values are publicly available from national statistic offices and the calculation is straightforward [1], [2], [3], [4].

text.text: Alternatively, mortality can be expressed as the Crude Mortality Rate (CMR), relating the number of deaths to the corresponding population size, or as an Age-Standardised Mortality Rate (ASMR), in which age-specific mortality rates are weighted according to a defined standard population.
These approaches differ substantially in their data requirements and in the assumptions required for their calculation.

A smaller number of authors use these measures to quantify excess mortality during the years of the COVID-19 pandemic [5], [6], [7], Regardless of the mortality measure used, expected mortality is commonly estimated by extrapolating mortality patterns observed during a pre-pandemic reference period which raises the question how to calculate the counterfactual number of deaths.

text.text: In aging populations, death counts are rising continuously and extrapolating existing trends is a straightforward approach.
Linear extrapolation makes the particularly simple assumption that the direction and magnitude of the observed trend keep the same and continue beyond the reference period.
Poisson regression is used in mortality surveillance systems such as EuroMOMO for modelling annual mortality trends [8].
text.formatted: Poisson regression is used in mortality surveillance systems such as EuroMOMO for modelling annual mortality trends <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: For the German pre-pandemic mortality data considered here, however, the gradual increase in annual deaths results in only minimal curvature of the exponential trend implied by Poisson regression.
Consequently, linear and Poisson regression yield very similar baseline estimates, with differences below 0.5% for all reference periods investigated [9].
text.formatted: Consequently, linear and Poisson regression yield very similar baseline estimates, with differences below 0.5% for all reference periods investigated <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Various national statistical offices used averages or median values of previous years rather than extrapolating an existing trend [10], [11].

text.text: In the presence of a rising mortality trend, such approaches result in a lower counterfactual baseline and consequently higher estimates of excess mortality.
More complex models implementing spline-based approaches, have been used by WHO and IHME to estimate the global mortality impact of the pandemic [1], [3].

text.text: While such models can account for nonlinear patterns within the observed period, extrapolation beyond the fitted data is also influenced by the estimated curvature.

Consequently, relatively small differences in curvature near the end of the reference period may result in substantially different counterfactual trajectories and these results have been discussed intensively [12].

text.text: Linear extrapolation avoids curvature and therefore provides a simple and transparent reference model.
As age standardisation is intended to remove the influence of differences in population age structure, the effect of population ageing is removed from the mortality trend.
This reveals the underlying longterm decline in age-specific mortality associated with increasing life expectancy, resulting in declining ASMR trends.
Analogous to increasing trends in death counts, such declining trends can be approximated and extrapolated linearly as well [7].
text.formatted: Analogous to increasing trends in death counts, such declining trends can be approximated and extrapolated linearly as well <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: This raises a fundamental methodological question: under which conditions does excess mortality derived from age-standardised mortality rates provide the same result as the substantially simpler calculation based directly on death counts?

Conversely, when the two approaches differ, it is important to understand whether these differences reflect the underlying mortality pattern or arise from the choice of standard population and age-group aggregation.
The present study investigates this relationship analytically and empirically.
The mathematical relationship between excess mortality derived from death counts and from ASMR is first established.
The effects of standard population and age-group aggregation are then examined using mortality in Germany during the COVID-19 pandemic as a case study.

Particular attention is given to the contrast between years in which excess mortality was concentrated in older age groups and years in which relative excess mortality was more broadly distributed across age groups.
Annual numbers of deaths in Germany, stratified by age, were obtained from the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) through the GENESIS database [13], [14].

In addition to the choice of standard population, the definition of the age groups affects ASMR-based excess mortality estimates.
To investigate this effect independently of the standard population, all calculations in this section use DE2020 as the standard population.
Table 3 compares calculations using 5-year age bands with 85+ or 80+ as the open-ended age group, as well as 10-year age bands with 80+ as the open-ended age group.
Changing the open-ended age group from 85+ to 80+, while retaining 5-year age bands for all younger ages, resulted in substantial differences in the estimated P-scores.
In 2020, the P-score decreased from 2.24% to 1.82%, whereas in 2022 it increased from 7.98% to 8.97% and in 2023 from 3.41% to 5.78%.
The effect is particularly relevant for 2020: using 85+ as the open-ended age group, the P-score of 2.24% exceeded the maximum deviation of 1.83% observed during the corresponding reference period.
With 80+ as the open-ended age group, however, the P-score of 1.82% remained below the corresponding reference-period maximum of 2.34%.
Thus, the definition of the open-ended age group changes the qualitative assessment of mortality in 2020 relative to the deviations observed during the reference period.

text.text: The dashed identity line indicates equal P-scores obtained from both approaches.
Baseline selection had a substantial effect on the estimated magnitude of excess mortality.
Nevertheless, both approaches responded systematically to changes in the reference period: baseline specifications producing higher death-count-based P-scores also produced higher ASMR-based Pscores.

The 2012-2019 and 2013-2019 reference periods, which yield estimates approximately in the middle of the range obtained from the investigated baseline specifications, also produced the closest agreement between both measures, with the corresponding P-scores located close to the identity line.
In contrast, the shorter 2015-2019 reference period produced markedly higher P-scores with both approaches, the reference period 2014-2019 produces lowest P-scores for both quantities.
For the other investigated reference periods, ASMR-based P-scores were consistently higher than the corresponding death-count-based estimates.
Thus, baseline selection affects not only the magnitude of estimated excess mortality but also the quantitative agreement between the two approaches.

Nevertheless, the systematic co-variation of both measures demonstrates that the choice of the prepandemic baseline is an important determinant of excess mortality estimates irrespective of whether they are derived from death counts or ASMR.
The analytical and empirical results demonstrate a close relationship between excess mortality derived from death counts and from age-standardised mortality rates.
Death-count-based relative excess mortality can be expressed as a weighted combination of age-specific excess mortality, with the expected numbers of deaths defining the weights.
ASMR-based excess mortality modifies these weights according to the relationship between the age distribution of the standard population and that of the population under study.
If both distributions are identical, both approaches yield the same relative excess mortality.
This relationship is reflected in the German data.
Although annual death counts increased during the pre-pandemic period while ASMR decreased, both approaches produced similar P-scores for 2020-2023.
Death counts therefore provide a comparatively simple and transparent measure of relative excess mortality when a single population is analysed over time.
The analytical relationship clarifies under which conditions both approaches provide similar results and why they may differ.
The choice of standard population affects ASMR-based excess mortality through the weighting of agespecific mortality.
The magnitude of this effect depends on the age distribution of excess mortality itself.

This explains the larger sensitivity observed in 2020, when excess mortality was strongly concentrated in the oldest age group, compared with 2022, when elevated mortality was distributed much more broadly across adult age groups.
The changing age pattern of excess mortality during the pandemic has also been demonstrated in the underlying age-stratified analysis.
The definition of the age groups introduces an additional and less obvious effect.
Aggregating 80-84 and 85+ into a single 80+ group leaves changes in age composition within this group unaccounted for by standardisation.
Because mortality differs substantially between 80-84 and 85+, such compositional changes affect the mortality rate of the aggregated group.
In contrast, when both groups are standardised separately, their relative weights are fixed by the standard population.
This distinction is particularly relevant for trend-based excess mortality estimates.
With DE2020 as the standard population, the aggregated and stratified calculations coincide when the age composition corresponds to that of 2020.
In earlier years, however, the population aged 80+ was relatively younger.
Consequently, aggregation changes the pre-pandemic ASMR trend and therefore the extrapolated expected mortality.
The resulting difference in the P-score is thus not primarily caused by the observed mortality in the target year, but by a different baseline.
This finding highlights an interaction between standard population and age-group definition.
A standard population can control changes in age structure only at the resolution provided by the selected age groups.

For trend-based excess mortality estimation, the standard population should therefore not be regarded merely as a scaling convention; together with the age-group definition, it determines which demographic changes are removed by standardisation and which remain in the mortality trend.
Baseline selection had a substantial influence on the magnitude of estimated excess mortality.
However, death-count-and ASMR-based P-scores responded in a closely corresponding manner when the reference period was varied.
The 2013-2019 baseline produced estimates approximately in the middle of the range obtained from the alternative reference periods.
This agrees with the previous sensitivity analysis, in which the 2013-2019 death-count trend yielded the median projected value and a slope close to the average of the investigated trends.
The 2015-2019 reference period provides a useful counterexample, producing markedly higher excess mortality estimates with both approaches.

Taken together, the results identify three closely related methodological choices affecting estimates of relative excess mortality: the baseline used to estimate expected mortality, the standard population used for age standardisation, and the age-group definition.
Death-count-based analysis avoids the latter two choices and therefore provides a useful transparent reference measure for analyses within a single population.

ASMR additionally controls for demographic change but introduces assumptions concerning standard population and age-group resolution that need to be reported and considered when interpreting trend-based excess mortality estimates.
The empirical analysis is limited to Germany and to the mortality patterns observed during 2020-2023.
The magnitude of the effects identified here may differ in populations with other age structures or mortality patterns.

Furthermore, the empirical calculations use linear baseline models, although the analytical relationships between death-count-and ASMR-based excess mortality are not restricted to the German pandemic period.

Population estimates used as denominators for age-specific mortality rates are themselves subject to demographic estimation and census revisions, providing an additional source of uncertainty in age-standardised analyses.
Death-count-and ASMR-based estimates of relative excess mortality are analytically closely related and can yield equivalent results under defined conditions.

The German data demonstrate that differences between the two approaches depend systematically on the standard population, the agegroup definition, and the baseline used to estimate expected mortality.
In particular, aggregation of the oldest age groups can alter the pre-pandemic ASMR trend by retaining 422 changes in age composition within the open-ended age group.
Consequently, age-group definition can 423 affect not only the level of an age-standardised mortality rate but also the resulting estimate of excess 424 mortality.
425 For analyses within a single population over time, death counts therefore provide a simple and 426 transparent reference measure.
More generally, excess mortality estimates should be interpreted in the 427 context of the baseline, standard population, and age-group definition from which they were derived.
